classification.difficultyReason: Interpret a scaled table, aggregate continent categories and express a subtotal as a percentage.

questions.mappingNote: Part a reads and scales one entry; part b sums the entries marked (A) and scales the result; part c applies the example's subset-over-total percentage method to the entries marked (E). The common scale factor cancels in part c.
questions.methodNote: Example 1 reads categories from a table and calculates a percentage as the relevant count divided by the appropriate total, multiplied by 100.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Interpret a scaled table, aggregate continent categories and express a subtotal as a percentage.

classification.difficultyReason: Read table entries, total capacities and form a staff-to-guests ratio.

questions.mappingNote: The ratio in part d is the most advanced directly assessed operation. The inspected teaching does not establish its prerequisite method.
questions.methodNote: Read the relevant row and column; combine table entries when a total is required. Page 2 demonstrates selecting the relevant quantities from a table.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Read table entries, total capacities and form a staff-to-guests ratio.

classification.difficultyReason: Aggregate match results into a summary table, compare totals and express a win count as a percentage.

questions.mappingNote: The final part directly assesses expressing one quantity as a percentage of another; earlier parts require tabulating and interpreting results.
questions.methodNote: Read and compare table entries. For a percentage, divide the relevant subgroup count by its total and multiply by 100, as in Example 1.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Aggregate match results into a summary table, compare totals and express a win count as a percentage.

classification.difficultyReason: Convert whole and half tree symbols using the key, total the farm frequencies, and use that total to calculate each requested percentage.

questions.mappingNote: Question 2 applies the pictogram key before summing frequencies and expressing a farm's frequency as a percentage of the total. Percentage calculation is the most advanced directly assessed skill; no percentage demonstration is supplied on these teaching pages.
questions.methodNote: Read each pictogram using its key, count repeated symbols of equal size and interpret a half-symbol as half the key value. Page 7 Example 3 explicitly demonstrates half-symbols.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Interpret whole and half pictogram symbols, total the frequencies and express selected frequencies as percentages.

classification.difficultyReason: Choose a common symbol value suited to the multiples of ten, then represent each cat frequency with consistent symbols and an explicit key.

questions.mappingNote: Question 4 directly applies the table-to-pictogram method. A key of 10 cats gives whole-symbol counts for all five categories.
questions.methodNote: Use repeated equal-sized symbols with an explicit key. Page 5 establishes a many-to-one symbol value; page 6 rejects varying symbol sizes; page 7 constructs a titled, labelled pictogram from a data table.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Construct a pictogram from a supplied table using a common symbol value.

classification.difficultyReason: Read heights using the intermediate grid intervals, recognise tied minimum years, and link the total births to the requested percentage.

questions.mappingNote: Question 2 applies the same graph-reading, total-frequency and part-of-total percentage methods as Example 4. Expressing a quantity as a percentage is the most advanced directly assessed skill.
questions.methodNote: Read bar heights using the labelled scale, add category frequencies to obtain the total, then divide the relevant frequency by the total and multiply by 100 to express it as a percentage, following Example 4.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Read a column graph, identify a tied minimum, total the frequencies and express one frequency as a percentage of the total.

classification.difficultyReason: Relate the sharp decline between January counts to the preceding July bushfire, then extend a plausible recent growth trend to predict when the population reaches 20 000.

questions.mappingNote: Question 3 extends the taught column-reading method to chronological data, requiring a conclusion about a July bushfire between January counts and a prediction from recent growth.
questions.methodNote: Read column heights using the labelled axis scale. Compare categories and quantities directly, as demonstrated in Example 4; apply differences to compare populations with 20 000.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Read a scaled column graph, infer the bushfire year from January observations, compare populations with a capacity and predict future growth.

classification.difficultyReason: Choose a suitable graph scale, classify chickens and geese as the two-legged subset, and calculate percentages using the total and the complement of sheep.

questions.mappingNote: Part a applies the taught graph conventions to the animal table. Parts b and c identify a subset and express its count as a percentage of all 50 animals; this is the most advanced directly assessed skill.
questions.methodNote: Page 9 teaches equal-width vertical or horizontal bars, a title, labelled axes and a numerical scale. Example 4 on page 10 totals the frequencies and calculates a percentage as the relevant frequency divided by the total, multiplied by 100%.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Construct a labelled graph and identify relevant animal groups before calculating percentages of the total.

classification.difficultyReason: Construct a scaled graph, identify which recorded times fall before 8:30, combine their frequencies for a percentage, and state a conclusion supported by the distribution.

questions.mappingNote: Question 5 applies these conventions to waking times, combines the three times before 8:30 a.m. for a percentage, and draws a conclusion from the frequencies.
questions.methodNote: Page 9 teaches equal-width vertical or horizontal bars, titles, labelled axes and scales. Example 4 on page 10 totals frequencies and calculates a category percentage as its frequency divided by the total, multiplied by 100%.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Construct a labelled graph, combine frequencies to calculate a percentage, and interpret the distribution.

classification.difficultyReason: Find the total sales, choose an overall bar length, and convert each category's share into a consecutive labelled segment.

questions.mappingNote: Question 2 applies the same proportional-length construction to car sales. The graph-representation skill is the closest catalogue match.
questions.methodNote: Example 5 calculates each segment length as category value divided by total, multiplied by an overall bar length of 10 cm, then constructs and labels the divided bar chart.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Calculate proportional segment lengths from four frequencies and construct a labelled divided bar chart.

classification.difficultyReason: Read column frequencies, find their total, convert each proportion to a sector angle and construct a labelled pie chart using the taught procedure.

questions.mappingNote: The task changes a six-category column display into a pie chart; represent-data-graphs is the closest supplied catalogue skill.
questions.methodNote: Read frequencies from the column heights. Pages 14 and 17 teach calculating each sector as frequency divided by total times 360 degrees, then constructing with a protractor and checking the angles sum to 360 degrees.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Read six frequencies from a column graph, calculate proportional sector angles and construct a labelled pie chart.

classification.difficultyReason: Calculate spending from the labelled percentages and explain why the larger percentage gives the smaller amount when the income bases differ; the earlier calculations scaffold this comparison.

questions.mappingNote: Parts a and b require percentage-of-quantity calculations using the clothes percentages printed on the two charts. Part c compares these amounts and their different income bases. Prerequisite teaching evidence remains missing.
questions.methodNote: Pages 14–17 explain pie-chart proportions, fraction-of-whole calculations and percentage representation. Page 10 calculates percentages from frequencies. None of these inspected pages explicitly teaches finding a percentage of an income.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Calculate expenditure from percentages and compare amounts when the total incomes differ.

classification.difficultyReason: Infer a missing sector angle and convert a sector's fraction of a full turn into a percentage.

questions.mappingNote: Part a compares sector sizes after finding the missing angle; part b subtracts known angles from 360 degrees; part c combines the taught sector-fraction and percentage methods. Expressing a quantity as a percentage is the most advanced directly assessed skill.
questions.methodNote: Pages 14–15 establish that sector angles total 360 degrees. Example 6 on pages 15–16 finds a fraction of the whole by dividing a sector angle by 360. Example 7 on pages 16–17 converts a fraction into a percentage by multiplying by 100.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Infer a missing sector angle and convert a sector's fraction of a full turn into a percentage.

classification.difficultyReason: Convert sector angles to population proportions, take a complement within the older male subgroup, and combine older groups with the middle-age percentage to find the remaining population before rounding.

questions.mappingNote: Question 8 interprets a pie chart to derive populations; part a additionally takes a complementary fraction, and part b subtracts the two older groups and the stated middle-age percentage.
questions.methodNote: Convert a sector angle to a fraction of the whole by dividing by 360, multiply by the total quantity, and use complementary fractions or categories. Retain exact intermediate values until the requested final rounding.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Combines sector fractions with population calculations, complementary groups and rounding.

classification.difficultyReason: Find weight gains by subtracting the birth weight, then choose scales and plot monthly weights using the taught line-graph method; additional points add repetition rather than new decisions.

questions.mappingNote: Part c directly applies Example 8 to monthly weight data; parts a and b subtract the initial weight from the relevant later weight.
questions.methodNote: Each point represents the measured value at a particular time; straight segments join successive points. Example 8 models a titled line graph with labelled axes and a uniform scale.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Calculate changes from a table and construct a labelled line graph using decimal weights.

classification.difficultyReason: Read endpoint balances and interpret each rising or falling weekly segment as an addition or withdrawal, excluding unchanged segments when counting.

questions.mappingNote: Starting and ending balances come from endpoint readings; additions and withdrawals correspond to rising and falling segments.
questions.methodNote: Read each point using the labelled scales. Connecting segments show increases, decreases or unchanged values over time.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Read initial and final balances and count rising and falling intervals.

classification.difficultyReason: Track countries through the legend, estimate a crossing year between plotted dates and compare total endpoint decreases rather than simply ranking final rates.

questions.mappingNote: The task extends the displayed line-graph reading method to comparing several series and estimating their intersection.
questions.methodNote: Read points against labelled axes and use connecting lines to interpret changes and trends.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Compare six plotted series, estimate an intersection year and compare changes over time.

classification.difficultyReason: Select a suitable temperature scale, label the axes and plot and join the seven supplied daily readings using the demonstrated method.

questions.mappingNote: Directly follows Example 8’s construction of a line graph from a day-by-day table.
questions.methodNote: Plot the tabulated observations in order, label both axes, select a suitable scale and join consecutive points.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Construct one line graph from seven explicitly tabulated values.

classification.difficultyReason: Read annual column heights, transfer them to a line graph and justify a representation by connecting its visual features to annual comparisons or change over time.

questions.mappingNote: Parts a and b combine the column-graph reading explanation with Example 8’s line-graph construction. Part c applies the stated purposes of the two graph types.
questions.methodNote: Read column heights using the vertical scale; plot ordered observations and join successive points for a line graph. Column graphs compare quantities; line graphs display trends and fluctuations.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Read a column graph, convert its data to a line graph and justify a choice of representation.

classification.difficultyReason: Interpret two journeys from a common distance reference, derive Keith's travelled distances from decreasing readings, convert minutes to hours and exclude his stop when calculating travelling average speed.

questions.mappingNote: Parts a–d use graphical readings and elapsed time. Parts e and f apply the average-speed method to complete or partial journeys, including exclusion of a stop. The supplied examples use whole hours and do not establish the prerequisite conversion from minutes to hours.
questions.methodNote: Read distances and times from a travel graph; horizontal segments show stops. Example 10 calculates average speed as distance travelled divided by time taken.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Interpret two journeys, convert minutes to hours and calculate average speed excluding a stop.

classification.difficultyReason: Interpret coincident journeys and return times, compare simultaneous distances to locate the greatest separation, and use the first two hours' travelled distance to calculate average speed.

questions.mappingNote: Parts a–d read and compare piecewise-linear distance–time graphs. Part e applies the demonstrated speed calculation using a whole-hour interval.
questions.methodNote: The travel-graph definition and bus examples teach reading distance and elapsed time, recognising horizontal stopping segments, and calculating average speed as distance travelled divided by time taken.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Compare two journeys, identify their greatest separation and calculate speed from a graph.

classification.difficultyReason: Read extrema from two graph series and compare their vertical differences across all twelve months.

questions.mappingNote: The question directly assesses interpretation of a two-series line graph, including extrema and differences; interpret-line-graphs is the closest supplied skill.
questions.methodNote: Pages 20–21 explain plotted temperatures, changes between points, peaks and troughs. Pages 9–10 support reading axis scales and comparing displayed quantities. Read each temperature series separately for extrema; compare vertical separations and subtract plotted values for differences.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Read extrema from two graph series and compare their vertical differences across all twelve months.

classification.difficultyReason: Organise predictions in a table, then combine five at-least-one-correct constraints to deduce a unique ordering.

questions.mappingNote: Part a applies table organisation directly. Part b uses the completed prediction table to draw conclusions by successive elimination, but the inspected teaching does not establish this deduction method.
questions.methodNote: Page 2 explains organising information by table categories and reading entries by row and column. Pages 9 and 10 explain constructing and interpreting column graphs; neither supplies a constraint-deduction demonstration.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Organise predictions in a table, then combine five at-least-one-correct constraints to deduce a unique ordering.

classification.difficultyReason: Requires choosing a suitable column scale and overall bar length, converting frequencies into proportional lengths and sector angles, and constructing labelled graphs. These are routine linked applications of taught methods with the total and graph types supplied; the six categories add repetition rather than insight.

questions.mappingNote: Question 4 applies these methods to the same six-faculty frequency table; representing data in three forms is its most advanced directly assessed skill.
questions.methodNote: Page 2 calculates percentages using part divided by relevant total times 100. Page 9 teaches equal-width column graphs with titles, labelled axes and scales. Page 13 calculates divided-bar lengths as category fraction times overall bar length. Pages 14 and 17 calculate pie-sector angles as category fraction times 360 degrees and construct sectors with a protractor.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Interpret a frequency table and represent the same six-category dataset using three different graphs, including proportional lengths and sector angles.

classification.difficultyReason: Read two journeys, convert minute intervals to hours and calculate speeds; interpret a stop and an intersection.

questions.mappingNote: Question 5 applies this graphical method to two journeys. Parts a and c additionally require conversion from minutes to hours; original prerequisite teaching evidence for that conversion was not supplied.
questions.methodNote: Example 10 reads distance and stopping intervals from a journey graph and calculates average speed as distance travelled divided by time taken. Its worked speed calculations use whole hours.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Read two journeys, convert minute intervals to hours and calculate speeds; interpret a stop and an intersection.

classification.difficultyReason: Interpret two multi-stage journeys, include stops in average speeds, and read a fractional intersection.

questions.mappingNote: Whole-journey average speed is the most advanced directly assessed skill in parts b and d. Other parts read distances, journey duration, stop duration and the intersection from distance–time graphs.
questions.methodNote: The travel-graph definition and bus example teach reading distance and elapsed time, recognising horizontal stops, adding outward and return distances, and calculating average speed as distance travelled divided by time taken. The example uses whole hours; prerequisite evidence for converting minutes to hours is missing.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Interpret two multi-stage journeys, include stops in average speeds, and read a fractional intersection.

bankProjection.note: Source-confirmed category headings are omitted only from bank prompts and presentation. Explicit equivalent fraction notation repairs satisfy bank validation. Source booklet content and all questions are retained.
